value.overview: The Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus) is a large, familiar plover of open ground, named for its loud, piercing call. Unlike many shorebirds, it often lives away from water and may use agricultural fields, roadsides, lawns, gravel areas, mudflats, and lake edges. Its two dark breast bands, long wings, orange lower back, and conspicuous distraction displays make it distinctive. In Costa Rica, it is chiefly a migrant and winter visitor, although small numbers may remain year-round and occasional breeding has been documented.
value.classification: The Killdeer belongs to the plover family Charadriidae and the order Charadriiformes. It is one of the larger North American plovers.
value.identification: Adults are brown above and white below, with a white forehead and throat separated by black markings and two bold black bands across the breast. The bill is short and dark, the legs are pinkish to dull orange, and the rump and upper tail show orange-brown coloration in flight. The species has a large-headed appearance, long pointed wings, and a loud, emphatic call often rendered as “kill-deer.” Juveniles are duller and lack the strong adult breast pattern.
value.rangeHabitat: The Killdeer breeds widely across Canada, the United States, and parts of Mexico, with additional populations farther south in the Americas. It uses open habitats with sparse vegetation, including beaches, mudflats, lake margins, short-grass fields, pasture, cropland, gravel lots, airfields, and disturbed urban areas. In Costa Rica it is recorded mainly in open lowland areas, wetlands, shorelines, agricultural landscapes, and other exposed ground during migration and winter. Small numbers may occur in the central highlands, where permanent residence and local breeding have been reported.
value.migrationStatus: Primarily a partial migrant. Many northern birds move south after breeding and occur in Costa Rica mainly during migration and the nonbreeding season, while some individuals remain year-round. Local breeding has been documented in Costa Rica, especially near suitable open ponds in the central highlands, but it is uncommon.
value.breeding: The nest is a shallow scrape on bare or sparsely vegetated ground, often surrounded by gravel, mud, short grass, or agricultural soil. Both adults may defend the nest and young, using the famous broken-wing display to lure predators away. The eggs are buff or stone-colored with dark markings and are incubated by both sexes. Precocial chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and are guided to feeding areas. Although chiefly a migrant in Costa Rica, breeding has been recorded there in small numbers.
value.dietFeeding: Killdeers feed mainly on ground-dwelling invertebrates, including beetles, flies, grasshoppers, caterpillars, worms, and other insects. They may also take spiders, small crustaceans, and occasionally seeds. The species usually forages by walking quickly across open ground, pausing to watch for prey before making short runs and pecks. It commonly feeds on muddy margins, short grass, disturbed soil, flooded fields, and shorelines, sometimes taking advantage of artificial lights or human-altered areas.
value.behavior: The Killdeer is active, alert, and highly vocal. It often runs rather than wades and may forage singly, in pairs, or in loose groups. Adults defend territories and nesting areas with calls, postures, and distraction displays. When threatened near a nest or brood, an adult may pretend to have an injured wing, drawing the danger away before flying off. Outside the breeding season, birds may gather in open fields and wetland margins, especially where food and bare ground are available.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining globally. The principal concern is a sustained reduction in abundance across much of the range rather than a small or highly localized distribution.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of open shorebird habitat, including wetlands, mudflats, beaches, grasslands, and agricultural areas, can reduce feeding and nesting opportunities. Nest and chick losses result from vehicles, livestock, recreation, pets, predators, mowing, cultivation, and other disturbance. Pollution, altered water regimes, and climate-related changes to wetlands and coastal habitats may add further pressure. In Costa Rica, disturbance and conversion of open wetland and agricultural habitats may affect migrants and the small local breeding population.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore wetlands, mudflats, beaches, ponds, grasslands, and other open habitats used by shorebirds. Keep dogs leashed near nesting or roosting areas, avoid driving on beaches and wetland margins, and respect seasonal signs and closures. Maintain undisturbed patches of bare or sparsely vegetated ground where the species breeds, and reduce mowing or farm work around active nests. Reporting sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs can help track distribution and population change.
